AIIB whistleblower sees China 'doubling down' on party control

Two years after he quit, Bob Pickard insists his allegations were not 'baseless'

Bob Pickard, a Canadian public relations veteran, went to work for the Beijing-headquartered Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank in 2022 but quit, complaining of a "toxic" culture dominated by the Chinese Communist Party. 

Kenji Kawase
June 14, 2025 15:01 JST

TOKYO - Exactly two years after Bob Pickard quit the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, saying it was "dominated" by Chinese Communist Party members, the Canadian whistleblower insists his claims were not "baseless" as the bank maintains.

Pickard, a public relations veteran who spoke with Nikkei Asia online from the western Canadian city of Calgary, said he sees Beijing "doubling down on party control" over the multilateral lender, which has 110 member states. "They call it multilateral, they call it international, but internally it really feels like a Chinese domestic bank, frankly," he said.

On June 14, 2023, Pickard announced on X his departure from his job as AIIB global communications director, complaining about the Communist Party's sway and saying the institution had "one of the most toxic cultures imaginable." He warned that Canada's interests were not served by its membership in the bank, which led to Ottawa launching a review and indefinitely suspending its participation.

AIIB President Jin Liqun in a recent interview with Nikkei Asia at the annual Future of Asia forum, dismissed Pickard's allegations as "baseless," repeating the bank's statement two years ago. He referred to an internal review published within a month of Pickard's resignation -- led by a Jin-appointed general counsel -- which "found no evidence to support or validate" the allegations and said the AIIB has an "apolitical, constructive, balanced and consensus-oriented decision culture."

Pickard questioned the review's seriousness. "Before any report, they called it 'baseless,'" he said.

The clashing views of Pickard and AIIB officials continue to cast a shadow on an institution that Beijing clearly considers part of its push for global influence and prestige, alongside its Belt and Road Initiative infrastructure-building program.

The AIIB was established in January 2016. At the twice-a-decade Chinese Communist Party Congress in October 2017, President Xi Jinping said his government had built the BRI and bank "jointly" as part of "all-round efforts in the pursuit of major country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics, thus advancing China's diplomatic agenda in a comprehensive, multilevel, multifaceted way and creating a favorable external environment for China's development."

Pickard believes there are "certain parallels or adjacency" in the AIIB and BRI, whereas Jin, the president, said "they are two different kinds of mechanisms or institutions."

Pickard said that in late 2021, he was "approached to help build a profile and a positive public image" for the AIIB.

Relations between China and Canada had been tense over the more than 1,000-day detention of two Canadian nationals -- Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, widely known as the "two Michaels." They were arrested in China shortly after Canadian authorities detained Meng Wanzhou, telecom equipment manufacturer Huawei Technologies' then chief financial officer and the founder's daughter, upon the request of the U.S.

But the Michaels were released in September 2021, and Pickard said his concerns over "undue influence" by China were allayed "somewhat" by the AIIB's governance rules and "assured" by the membership of democracies, including Canada. He joined the bank in March 2022, bringing his experience at global public relations firms like Edelman and Burson-Marsteller, coupled with 16 years of engagement with Asia.

It did not take long for Pickard to discover the reality, as he sees it. "Inside of the bank, CCP members wield power in many of the most powerful positions," he told the parliamentary committee of the Canadian House of Commons after his return from China. This includes Jin, who according to Pickard, "often articulates Chinese government policy as if it were his own."

Jin, in his interview with Nikkei Asia, acknowledged that China holds "a de facto veto power" since it owns over 25% of the bank's voting rights. But he also emphasized that the aggregate voting rights of Europeans and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development members also exceed 25%. He said there are built-in "checks and balances" and that the near-doubling of the bank's membership since its inception shows its inclusiveness.

As Jin's decade-long tenure will end in January, China has nominated Zou Jiayi as its candidate to succeed him. She is a deputy secretary-general of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, or CPPCC, the country's top political advisory body, and one of the Communist Party's 200-plus central committee members.

Pickard suggested that this shows Beijing's tightening control.

While both Jin and Zou are former vice finance ministers, Pickard said, "Arguably, she is more political than he is." While Jin had experience working outside the Chinese-controlled system -- at the World Bank in Washington and as the first Chinese national to be the vice president of the Asian Development Bank in Manila -- Pickard said published details on Zou's background show no positions with "political independence."

"In choosing her, they are sending a strong signal that the party and Chinese control is more powerful than ever," he said, while China is essentially "dropping any pretense" that the bank is independent.

Zou is widely expected to be elected at the AIIB's annual meeting later this month in Beijing. Jin would neither comment on the succession nor on Zou, saying, "I don't want to be perceived ... the bank is not to be perceived as using its own influence to do or say anything, which would affect the outcome."

Looking back on his experience two years ago, Pickard recalled the slew of criticism that followed his resignation in mainland Chinese media, which he called a "standard whistleblower smearing campaign."

But Pickard, now principal at Toronto-based Leadership Communication, said the experience "made me a better PR consultant because I walked through a fire. I am now more experienced, as I have endured these attacks."

As for the AIIB's outlook, he believes U.S. President Donald Trump is giving China "a wonderful propaganda gift" as it seeks to brand itself and its institutions as responsible global actors. With Washington shunning multilateralism and the Trump administration's economic policies unsettling friends and foes alike, "Chaos in the U.S. is a golden opportunity for AIIB," Pickard said.
